clue.text: April 1815 — Statesman

parts.note: a general-knowledge clue: a statesman born in April 1815, the Prussian who unified Germany

explanation.walkthrough: This puzzle's dated clues each give a famous person's job and a month and year from their life, usually the birth.
explanation.definitionFit: Otto von Bismarck, the Iron Chancellor of Germany, was born on 1 April 1815.

clue.text: Wooster, officially Count of Rousillon

definitions.meaning: Bertie Wooster, P. G. Wodehouse's hero, has a full formal first name of which Bertie is the pet form
the young count who spurns Helena in Shakespeare's All's Well That Ends Well

explanation.surface: Wodehouse's Wooster given a formal French noble title.
explanation.definitionFit: Bertie is short for the full name, and Shakespeare gives the same name to the reluctant husband in All's Well.

clue.text: Small painful lesion, one that comes with time according to Hamlet

definitions.text: one that comes with time according to Hamlet

parts.note: S is the usual abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
a corn is a painful hard patch of skin on the foot

explanation.surface: A small sore, and a line from Hamlet about what time brings.
explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet's 'To be or not to be' speech asks who would bear 'the whips and scorns of time'.
explanation.definitionFit: Contempt is one of the burdens Hamlet lists alongside time's whips in his soliloquy.

clue.text: Tune accompanied by angels, according to Hill

definitions.text: accompanied by angels, according to Hill
definitions.meaning: Susan Hill's 1991 novel is titled with this word paired with angels

explanation.surface: A melody sung with a heavenly choir, as a writer describes it.
explanation.definitionFit: A tune is a melody, and Susan Hill's novel 'Air and Angels' borrows its title from a Donne poem.

clue.text: Edward, say, Saint thus included in talk

indicators.note: the saint and the word for thus are placed inside the word for talk

parts.note: to confer is to talk things over
so means thus, in this way

explanation.surface: King Edward, a saint, mentioned in conversation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Edward, say' points to Edward the Confessor, the English king and saint; 'say' marks him as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: King Edward the Confessor is an example of one who professes the faith, the title given to that saint-king.

clue.text: June 1826 — Composer

parts.note: a general-knowledge clue: a German composer who died in London in June 1826

explanation.walkthrough: Unlike most dated clues here, this date is the composer's death, not birth.
explanation.definitionFit: Carl Maria von Weber, composer of Der Freischütz, died in London on 5 June 1826.

clue.text: Lawrence's fifth novel I'm now reviewing

definitions.text: Lawrence's fifth novel I'm now reviewing

indicators.note: a reviewer goes over a book again, so the letters are looked at afresh in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: take only the fifth letter of the name Lawrence

explanation.surface: A critic says they are reviewing D. H. Lawrence's fifth novel.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines and builds the answer: E from 'Lawrence's fifth' joins NOVELIMNOW and 'reviewing' rearranges them.
explanation.definitionFit: D. H. Lawrence's novel of 1920 about the Brangwen sisters followed The Rainbow as his fifth.

clue.text: January 1655 — Mathematician

parts.note: a general-knowledge clue: a Swiss mathematician born in January 1655 by the new calendar

explanation.definitionFit: Jacob Bernoulli, eldest of the Swiss family of mathematicians, was born in Basel in early January 1655.

clue.text: Defies the Weird Sisters

indicators.note: weird means strange or odd, so the letters of the next word are rearranged oddly

explanation.surface: Someone stands up to the witches in Macbeth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Weird Sisters' are the witches in Macbeth, but 'Weird' is the anagram signal on SISTERS.
explanation.definitionFit: To resist is to oppose or withstand, the same as to defy.

clue.text: Mostly strange subject for Conor McPherson

indicators.note: most of the word is kept, its final letter dropped

parts.note: weird means strange

explanation.surface: Something odd as a topic for an Irish playwright.
explanation.walkthrough: Conor McPherson's play 'The Weir' (1997) is set in a rural Irish pub.
explanation.definitionFit: A low river dam is the title subject of McPherson's best-known play.

clue.text: Lambert's cantata — you can bank on it!

definitions.meaning: Constant Lambert's 1927 choral work for piano, chorus and orchestra, named after an American river
a river has banks, so one could stand on its bank

explanation.surface: A composer's choral piece described as a sure bet.
explanation.definitionFit: Lambert set a Sacheverell Sitwell poem named after the great river of the US–Mexico border; any river has banks.

clue.text: Customs written about in verse romance

indicators.note: about signals a turnaround, so the letters found are read in the opposite direction
the letters sit inside the words verse romance

explanation.surface: Social habits described in a medieval poem.
explanation.walkthrough: SEROM spans 'verSE ROMance'; 'about' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin plural for a society's customs and conventions is used in English for accepted ways of behaving.

clue.text: Group verse delivered by children gambolling

indicators.note: the letters are given out by the phrase that follows, sitting within it

explanation.surface: A poem recited by playful children.
explanation.definitionFit: Japanese linked verse is composed by several poets in turn, each adding stanzas.

clue.text: Exploit a note about Miss Arden by servants

indicators.note: the note goes around the rest, enclosing the actress and the servants

parts.note: a chit is a short note

indicators.note: by means next to, so the servants are placed beside the actress

parts.note: Eve Arden was an American actress, star of Our Miss Brooks
men can mean servants or retainers

explanation.surface: A memo concerning an actress and her household staff.
explanation.definitionFit: An exploit is a notable deed, a feat accomplished.

clue.text: Ecstasy's destroyed our reason, lacking a bit of awareness. Wrong!

parts.note: E is the slang abbreviation for the drug ecstasy

indicators.note: something destroyed is wrecked, so these letters are broken up and rebuilt
the letters of our reason go without one letter
only the first letter of awareness is taken

explanation.surface: A warning that drugs ruin the mind and take away awareness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lacking' removes A (from 'a bit of awareness') from OURREASON; with E that leaves EOURRESON for 'destroyed' to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Erroneous means mistaken or incorrect.

clue.text: February 1766- Demographer

parts.note: a general-knowledge clue: an English population theorist born in February 1766

explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Robert Malthus, author of An Essay on the Principle of Population, was born on 13 February 1766.

clue.text: Tingling all over and needing hospital when struck by this

indicators.note: all over the place, so the letters are scattered and rearranged

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hospital, as on road signs

explanation.surface: Someone tingling everywhere and needing hospital after a bolt from the sky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'all over' rearranges TINGLING plus the H for hospital.
explanation.definitionFit: A flash of atmospheric electricity is what strikes a person in a storm.

clue.text: Row with Patterson, cultural attaché, festers

parts.note: a rank is a row, as of soldiers or taxis
Sir Les Patterson, Barry Humphries' boorish comic creation, is Australia's cultural attaché

explanation.surface: A quarrel with a diplomat leaves a lingering grievance.
explanation.walkthrough: Barry Humphries, the Australian comedian behind Dame Edna, also played the crude diplomat Les Patterson.
explanation.definitionFit: A grievance that rankles keeps irritating, as a wound that festers keeps causing pain.

clue.text: Le Roi got partly transformed, transformed into this opera

indicators.note: transformed means changed in form, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: only part of the word transformed, its first letter, is used

explanation.surface: Hugo's play Le Roi s'amuse turned into a Verdi opera.
explanation.walkthrough: Verdi's opera was adapted from Victor Hugo's play 'Le Roi s'amuse'; T from 'partly transformed' joins LEROIGOT to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Verdi's 1851 opera about a court jester is the work Hugo's play became.

clue.text: "What have I done to be made a — of?" (Old Curiosity Shop)

definitions.text: "What have I done to be made a — of?" (Old Curiosity Shop)

parts.words: "What have I done to be made a — of?" (Old Curiosity Shop)
parts.note: a quotation from Dickens to complete: the missing word is a thing of dread or annoyance

explanation.definitionFit: A source of persistent dread or irritation fits the gap in Dickens's line.

clue.text: Stream, and in French, last part of Godot; he'd approve

parts.note: a beck is a northern English word for a stream
et is French for and

indicators.note: only the final letter of Godot is taken

explanation.surface: A stream and a French phrase tied to the end of a famous play whose author would approve.
explanation.walkthrough: Waiting for Godot is by Samuel Beckett, who wrote it in French; hence the author approving of a clue built from French and Godot.
explanation.definitionFit: The playwright of Waiting for Godot would endorse a clue so full of his own work.

clue.text: May 1883 — Architect

parts.note: a general-knowledge clue: a German architect born in May 1883, founder of the Bauhaus

explanation.definitionFit: Walter Gropius, who founded the Bauhaus school, was born in Berlin on 18 May 1883.

clue.text: Erstwhile prison where you might have seen a post-punk ballet

definitions.meaning: the Berlin jail, demolished in 1987, that held Nazi war criminals

definitions.text: where you might have seen a post-punk ballet
definitions.meaning: the 1980s New Romantic band took the prison's name with Ballet added

explanation.surface: A former jail now hosting an avant-garde dance show.
explanation.definitionFit: The Berlin prison that held Rudolf Hess gave its name to the band Spandau Ballet.

clue.text: Beat up herald at Canterbury initially, where a murder occurred

indicators.note: only the first letter of Canterbury is used
beaten up means battered, so the letters are knocked into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A messenger is attacked in Canterbury.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Becket was murdered in Canterbury Cathedral in 1170; C from 'Canterbury initially' joins HERALDAT for 'Beat up' to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Archbishop Becket was killed in the great church at Canterbury, the scene of that famous murder.

clue.text: It's not often an artist disappears, depend on it

indicators.note: the artist vanishes from the word for not often

parts.note: rarely means not often
RA is a Royal Academician, a member of the Royal Academy of Arts

explanation.surface: Artists seldom vanish, and you can count on that.
explanation.definitionFit: To rely on something is to trust or count on it.

clue.text: A slave from Stowe becoming a London flower girl

definitions.meaning: the enslaved mother who flees across the ice in Harriet Beecher Stowe's Uncle Tom's Cabin
the Cockney heroine of Shaw's Pygmalion, surnamed Doolittle

explanation.surface: An enslaved woman from an American novel reinvented as a Covent Garden flower seller.
explanation.definitionFit: The same first name belongs to Stowe's escaping slave and Shaw's Doolittle.

clue.text: Jack Sparrow, for instance, loses his head and gets angry

indicators.note: the first letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: Captain Jack Sparrow is the buccaneer of the Pirates of the Caribbean films

explanation.surface: A film buccaneer is beheaded and becomes furious.
explanation.definitionFit: Irate means very angry.

clue.text: One-time French island Camus wrote about

parts.note: ex means former
île is French for island

explanation.surface: A former French island in Camus's writing.
explanation.walkthrough: Camus's story collection 'L'Exil et le royaume' is translated 'Exile and the Kingdom'.
explanation.definitionFit: Banishment from one's homeland is the theme of Camus's 1957 collection.

clue.text: "Oxford, that -, saps the will-power, the power of action" (Zuleika Dobson)

definitions.text: "Oxford, that -, saps the will-power, the power of action" (Zuleika Dobson)

parts.words: "Oxford, that -, saps the will-power, the power of action" (Zuleika Dobson)
parts.note: a quotation from Max Beerbohm's novel to complete: the missing phrase is a place of dreamy idleness

explanation.definitionFit: A place of languid ease, after the flower-eaters of Homer's Odyssey, fits Beerbohm's view of Oxford.

clue.text: Relation by principal characters in Sorrow in Sunlight

indicators.note: the leading letters of each word are taken

explanation.surface: A relative mentioned in a Firbank novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sorrow in Sunlight' is a Ronald Firbank novel; 'characters' means letters, not people.
explanation.definitionFit: A sister is a family relation, shortened here.

clue.text: You get this tense after the first part of a Harlan Coben thriller

definitions.text: after the first part of a Harlan Coben thriller
definitions.meaning: Coben's 2008 novel is Hold ___, so this word follows its first part

explanation.surface: A thriller leaves the reader on edge.
explanation.definitionFit: Tense means taut or strained, and Coben's novel is titled Hold Tight.

clue.text: June 1712 — Philosopher

parts.note: a general-knowledge clue: a Genevan philosopher born in June 1712, author of The Social Contract

explanation.definitionFit: Jean-Jacques Rousseau, author of The Social Contract, was born in Geneva on 28 June 1712.
